{{Short description|Technique used in perturbation theory}}
In [[perturbation theory]], the '''Poincaré–Lindstedt method''' or '''Lindstedt–Poincaré method''' is a technique for uniformly approximating [[periodic function|periodic]] solutions to [[ordinary differential equation]]s, when regular perturbation approaches fail. The method removes [[Secular variation|secular terms]]—terms growing without bound—arising in the straightforward application of [[perturbation theory]] to weakly [[nonlinear]] problems with finite oscillatory solutions.<ref>{{citation | first=P.G. | last=Drazin | title=Nonlinear systems | publisher=Cambridge University Press | year=1992 | isbn=0-521-40668-4 | url-access=registration | url=https://archive.org/details/nonlinearsystems0000draz }}, pp. 181–186.</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Strogatz |first=Steven |title=Nonlinear dynamics and chaos : with applications to physics, biology, chemistry, and engineering |date=2019 |isbn=978-0-367-09206-1 |edition=2nd |location=Boca Raton |chapter=Exercise 7.6.19, 7.6.21 |oclc=1112373147}}</ref>

The method is named after [[Henri Poincaré]],<ref>{{citation | first=H. | last=Poincaré | authorlink=Henri Poincaré | title=Les Méthodes Nouvelles de la Mécanique Célèste | volume=II | publisher=Dover Publ. | location=New York | year=1957 | orig-date=1893 }}, §123–§128.</ref> and [[Anders Lindstedt]].<ref>A. Lindstedt, Abh. K. Akad. Wiss. St. Petersburg 31, No. 4 (1882)</ref>

{{Blockquote|text=All efforts of geometers in the second half of this century have had as main objective the elimination of secular terms.|title=Les Méthodes Nouvelles de la Mécanique Céleste|author=[[Henri Poincaré]]|source=preface to volume I}}The article gives several examples. The theory can be found in Chapter 10 of Nonlinear Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems by Verhulst.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Verhulst |first=Ferdinand |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-642-61453-8 |title=Nonlinear Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems |date=1996 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-540-60934-6 |series=Universitext |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-61453-8}}</ref>

==Example: the Duffing equation==
The undamped, unforced [[Duffing equation]] is given by

:<math>\ddot{x} + x + \varepsilon\, x^3 = 0\,</math>

for ''t''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0, with 0&nbsp;<&nbsp;''ε''&nbsp;≪&nbsp;1.<ref name=logan>J. David Logan. ''Applied Mathematics'', Second Edition, John Wiley & Sons, 1997. {{ISBN|0-471-16513-1}}.</ref>
 
Consider initial conditions

:<math>x(0) = 1,\,</math> {{pad|5em}} <math> \dot x(0) = 0.\,</math>

A [[perturbation theory|perturbation-series]] solution of the form ''x''(''t'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x''<sub>0</sub>(''t'')&nbsp;+&nbsp;''ε''&nbsp;''x''<sub>1</sub>(''t'')&nbsp;+&nbsp;... is sought. The first two terms of the series are

:<math>x(t) = \cos(t) + \varepsilon \left[ \tfrac{1}{32}\, \left( \cos(3t) - \cos(t) \right) - \tfrac{3}{8}\, t\, \sin(t) \right] + \cdots.\,</math>

This approximation grows without bound in time, which is inconsistent with the [[physical system]] that [[Duffing equation|the equation]] models.<ref>The Duffing equation has an invariant energy <math>\scriptstyle E=\tfrac12\, \dot{x}^2 + \tfrac12\, x^2 + \tfrac14\, \varepsilon\, x^4</math>&nbsp;=&nbsp;constant, as can be seen by multiplying the Duffing equation with <math>\scriptstyle \dot{x}</math> and integrating with respect to time&nbsp;''t''. For the example considered, from its initial conditions, is found: ''E''&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{sfrac|1|2}}&nbsp;+&nbsp;{{sfrac|1|4}}&nbsp;''ε''.</ref> The term responsible for this unbounded growth, called the '''secular term'''<!-- [[secular term]] redirects here-->, is <math>t\sin(t)</math>. The Poincaré–Lindstedt method allows for the creation of an approximation that is accurate for all time, as follows.

In addition to expressing the solution itself as an [[asymptotic series]], form another series with which to scale time ''t'':

:<math>\tau = \omega t,\,</math> {{pad|4em}} where {{pad|4em}} <math>\omega = \omega_0 + \varepsilon \omega_1 + \cdots.\,</math>

We have the [[leading-order|leading order]] <math>\omega_0 = 1</math>, because when <math>\varepsilon = 0</math>, the equation has solution <math>x = \cos (t)</math>. Then the original problem becomes

:<math>\omega^2\, x''(\tau) + x(\tau) + \varepsilon\, x^3(\tau) = 0\,</math>

Now search for a solution of the form ''x''(''τ'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x''<sub>0</sub>(''τ'')&nbsp;+&nbsp;''ε''&nbsp;''x''<sub>1</sub>(''τ'')&nbsp;+&nbsp;...&nbsp;. The following solutions for the zeroth and first order problem in <math>\varepsilon</math> are obtained:

:<math>
  \begin{align}
    x_0 &= \cos(\tau) \\
    \text{and }
    x_1 &= \tfrac{1}{32}\, \left(\cos(3\tau)-\cos(\tau)\right) + \left( \omega_1 - \tfrac{3}{8}  \right)\, \tau\, \sin(\tau).
  \end{align}
</math>

So the secular term can be removed through the choice: ''ω''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;<small>{{sfrac|3|8}}</small>. Higher orders of accuracy can be obtained by continuing the perturbation analysis along this way. As of now, the approximation—correct up to first order in ''ε''—is

:<math>
  x(t) \approx \cos\Bigl(\left(1 + \tfrac{3}{8}\, \varepsilon \right)\, t \Bigr) 
             + \tfrac{1}{32}\, \varepsilon\, \left[\cos\Bigl( 3 \left(1 + \tfrac{3}{8}\,\varepsilon\, \right)\, t \Bigr)-\cos\Bigl(\left(1 + \tfrac{3}{8}\,\varepsilon\, \right)\, t \Bigr)\right]. \,
</math>

== Example: the van der Pol oscillator ==
We solve the van der Pol oscillator only up to order 2. This method can be continued indefinitely in the same way, where the order-n term <math>\epsilon^n x_n</math> consists of a harmonic term <math>a_n\cos(t) + b_n\cos(t)</math>, plus some super-harmonic terms <math>a_{n, 2}\cos(2t) + b_{n, 2}\cos(2t) + \cdots.</math> The coefficients of the super-harmonic terms are solved directly, and the coefficients of the harmonic term are determined by expanding down to order-(n+1), and eliminating its secular term.

See chapter 10 of <ref name=":0" /> for a derivation up to order 3, and <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Andersen |first1=C. M. |last2=Geer |first2=James F. |date=June 1982 |title=Power Series Expansions for the Frequency and Period of the Limit Cycle of the Van Der Pol Equation |url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/0142047 |journal=SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics |language=en |volume=42 |issue=3 |pages=678–693 |doi=10.1137/0142047 |issn=0036-1399|url-access=subscription }}</ref> for a computer derivation up to order 164.

Consider the [[van der Pol oscillator]] with equation<math display="block">\ddot x + \epsilon (x^2-1) \dot x + x = 0</math>where <math>\epsilon</math> is a small positive number. Perform substitution to the second order:<blockquote><math>\tau = \omega t,\,</math> {{pad|4em}} where {{pad|4em}} <math>\omega = 1 + \epsilon \omega_1 + \epsilon^2 \omega_2 + O(\epsilon^3)</math></blockquote>which yields the equation<math display="block">\omega^2\ddot x + \omega\epsilon (x^2-1) \dot x + x = 0</math>Now plug in <math>x = x_0 + \epsilon x_1 + \epsilon^2 x_2 + O(\epsilon^3)</math>, and we have three equations, for the orders <math>1, \epsilon, \epsilon^2</math> respectively:<math display="block">\begin{cases}
\ddot x_0 + x_0 = 0 \\
\ddot x_1 + x_1 + 2\omega_1 \ddot x_0 + (x_0^2-1)\dot x_0 = 0 \\
\ddot x_2 + x_2 + (\omega_1^2 + 2\omega_2)\ddot x_0 + 2\omega_1 \ddot x_1 + 2x_0x_1\dot x_0 + \omega_1(x_0^2-1)\dot x_0 + \dot x_1(x_0^2-1) = 0
\end{cases}</math>The first equation has general solution <math>x_0 =A \cos (\tau + \phi)</math>. Pick origin of time such that <math>\phi = 0</math>. Then plug it into the second equation to obtain (after some trigonometric identities)<math display="block">\ddot x_1 + x_1 + (A-A^3/4) \sin\tau - 2\omega_1 A \cos \tau - (A^3/4) \sin(3\tau) = 0</math>To eliminate the secular term, we must set both <math>\sin\tau, \cos \tau</math> coefficients to zero, thus we have <math display="block">\begin{cases}
A= A^3/4 \\
2\omega_1 A = 0
\end{cases}</math>yielding <math>A = 2, \omega_1  = 0</math>. In particular, we found that when <math>\epsilon</math> increases from zero to a small positive constant, all circular orbits in [[phase space]] are destroyed, except the one at radius 2. Now solving <math>\ddot x_1 + x_1 = 2\sin(3\tau)</math> yields <math>x_1 = B \cos(\tau + \phi) -\frac 14 \sin(3\tau)</math>. We can always absorb <math>\epsilon B\cos(\tau + \phi)</math> term into <math>x_0</math>, so we can WLOG have just <math>x_1 = -\frac 14 \sin(3\tau)</math>.

Now plug into the second equation to obtain<math display="block">\ddot x_2 + x_2 -(4\omega_2 + 1/4)\cos\tau - \frac 34 \cos 3\tau - \frac 54 \cos 5\tau = 0</math>To eliminate the secular term, we set <math>\omega_2 = -\frac{1}{16}</math>.

Thus we find that <math>\omega = 1 - \frac{1}{16}\epsilon^2 + O(\epsilon^3)</math>.

== Example: Mathieu equation ==
This is an example of [[parametric resonance]].

Consider the [[Mathieu equation]] <math>\ddot x + (1 + b\epsilon^2 + \epsilon \cos(t))x = 0</math>, where <math>b</math> is a constant, and <math>\epsilon</math> is small. The equation's solution would have two time-scales, one fast-varying on the order of <math>t</math>, and another slow-varying on the order of <math>T = \epsilon^2 t</math>. So expand the solution as <math display="block">x(t) = x_0(t, T) + \epsilon x_1(t, T) + \epsilon^2 x_2(t, T) + O(\epsilon^3)</math>Now plug into the Mathieu equation and expand to obtain<math display="block">\begin{cases}
\partial_t^2 x_0 + x_0 = 0 \\
\partial_t^2 x_1 + x_1 = -\cos(t)x_0 \\
\partial_t^2 x_2 + x_2 = -bx_0 - 2\partial_{tT}x_0 - \cos(t)x_1
\end{cases}</math>As before, we have the solutions<math display="block">\begin{cases}
x_0 = A\cos(t) + B \sin(t) \\
x_1 = -\frac A2 + \frac A6 \cos(2t) + \frac B6 \sin(2t)
\end{cases}</math>The secular term coefficients in the third equation are <math display="block">\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{12} \left(-12 b A+5 A-24 B'\right) \\
\frac{1}{12} \left(24 A'-12 b B-B\right)
\end{cases}</math>Setting them to zero, we find the equations of motion:

<math>\frac{d}{dT} \begin{bmatrix}
A \\ B
\end{bmatrix} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & \frac 12 (\frac{1}{12} + b) \\
\frac 12 (\frac{5}{12} - b) & 0 \\
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
A\\B
\end{bmatrix}</math>

Its determinant is <math>\frac 14 (b-5/12) (b + 1/12)</math>, and so when <math>b \in (-1/12, 5/12)</math>, the origin is a saddle point, so the amplitude of oscillation <math>\sqrt{A^2 + B^2}</math> grows unboundedly.

In other words, when the [[angular frequency]] (in this case, <math>1</math>) in the parameter is sufficiently close to the angular frequency (in this case, <math>\sqrt{1+b\epsilon^2 }</math>) of the original oscillator, the oscillation grows unboundedly, like a child swinging on a swing pumping all the way to the moon.

== Shohat expansion ==

For the van der Pol oscillator, we have <math>\omega \sim 1/\epsilon</math> for large <math>\epsilon</math>, so as <math>\epsilon</math> becomes large, the serial expansion of <math>\omega</math> in terms of <math>\epsilon</math> diverges and we would need to keep more and more terms of it to keep <math>\omega</math> bounded. This suggests to us a parametrization that is bounded:<math display="block">r := \frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}</math>Then, using serial expansions <math>\epsilon \omega = r + c_2 r^2 + c_3 r^3 + c_4 r^4 + \cdots</math> and <math>x = x_0 + r x_1 + r^2 x_2 + \cdots</math>, and using the same method of eliminating the secular terms, we find <math>c_2 = 1, c_3 = \frac{15}{16}, c_4 = \frac{13}{16}</math>.

Because <math>\lim_{\epsilon \to \infty}r = 1</math>, the expansion <math>\epsilon \omega = r + c_2 r^2 + c_3 r^3 + c_4 r^4 + \cdots</math> allows us to take a finite number of terms for the series on the right, and it would converge to a finite value at <math>\epsilon \to \infty</math> limit. Then we would have <math>\omega \sim 1/\epsilon</math>, which is exactly the desired asymptotic behavior. This is the idea behind Shohat expansion<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bellman |first=Richard |title=Perturbation techniques in mathematics, engineering & physics |date=2003 |publisher=Dover Publications |isbn=0-486-43258-0 |location=Mineola, N.Y. |chapter=2.5. The Shohat Expansion |oclc=51942387}}</ref>.

The exact asymptotic constant is <math>\epsilon\omega \to \frac{2\pi}{3-2\ln 2} = 3.8936\cdots </math>, which as we can see is approached by <math>1 + c_2 + c_3 + c_4 = 3.75</math>.
